title: How DST schedules and checks a run — code review

sections.heading: 1. How can the simulator see stopped calls?

notes.text: The simulator needs both ends of a handoff to know what it can advance or drop.
The harness exposes a snapshot of calls currently held by a gate.
Each call contributes at most one current stop. The scheduler never receives stale stops.
Finished calls and calls already being controlled are excluded; every returned call is actionable.

sections.heading: 2. How does one step leave other work in flight?

notes.text: Before: one commit ran to completion within the step, so another write could not overlap it.
Now a write starts and stays in flight. A later step may start another write or advance this one.
At each step, the simulator refreshes the list of calls it can act on.
The cap still allows a second mutation while the first call is paused.
Advance releases just this call's current gate; the backend alone does not choose the whole interleaving.

sections.heading: 3. What does an enabled event do to the test world?

notes.text: The world gives each stopped call a stable name for the saved trace and replay.
A set or remove begins a local client write.
Advance releases one handoff. The promise remains in flight if it later stops again.
Drop fails that exact handoff, simulating a lost network message.
Restart creates a new client incarnation over its durable storage.
After each event settles, compare observed state with an independent model.

sections.heading: 4. What state should the clients and server have?

notes.text: The model tracks server state independently from Tandem's implementation.
A local write remains pending until a pull acknowledges it.
Only mutations the server actually accepted change expected server state.
An acknowledgement removes only writes through the acknowledged mutation.
Expected client state combines its last received server state with its own unacknowledged writes.

sections.heading: 5. Which handoffs may a fault drop?

notes.text: Before: anything that was not a timer, including a local storage write, could be dropped.
Now only calls crossing the client/server boundary enter the fault lottery.

sections.heading: 6. How is a network handoff identified?

notes.text: The old predicate could only rule out timer calls; it said nothing about disk writes.
A request, response, or poke has the server on one side. Timers and local storage do not.

sections.heading: 7. How does a saved failure run again?

notes.text: Replay reads the recorded choice for this step instead of asking the random generator again.
If that event is no longer possible, replay reports the first point of divergence.
The same event is applied to a fresh world.
The same independent check should reproduce the bug at the same step.
